content: Bacterial pneumonia is a lung infection caused by bacteria. The most common bacterial pathogen responsible for pneumonia across all age groups, except newborns, is Streptococcus pneumoniae. This is a gram-positive bacterium that often resides harmlessly in the throat of healthy individuals. Another significant gram-positive bacterium causing pneumonia is Staphylococcus aureus. Gram-negative bacteria, though less frequently implicated, include Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Moraxella catarrhalis. These gram-negative organisms often originate in the gastrointestinal tract and can enter the lungs when gastric contents, such as vomit, are aspirated. Atypical bacteria, such as Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila, are so named because they tend to cause milder forms of pneumonia, often referred to as walking pneumonia, and are more common in teenagers and young adults. These atypical pathogens also require different antibiotic treatments compared to typical bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae. Historically, bacterial pneumonia has been recognized as a severe infectious disease. It was a major cause of mortality during the 1918 Influenza Pandemic and was often referred to as the captain of the men of death. The causative agent Streptococcus pneumoniae was first isolated in 1880 by Louis Pasteur and George Sternberg. Before the advent of antibiotics, treatments such as bloodletting were commonly employed, as described by William Osler in his 1892 textbook The Principles and Practice of Medicine. The introduction of modern antibiotics has revolutionized the management of bacterial pneumonia. Bacterial pneumonia develops when causative bacteria are inhaled from the environment or migrate from the upper respiratory tract, where they may already reside. Once the bacteria reach the alveoli, the immune system responds by mobilizing white blood cells, particularly neutrophils, to the site of infection. This immune response, while essential for clearing the infection, also produces systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, and fatigue. If the bacteria enter the bloodstream, they can cause sepsis, potentially affecting other organs like the brain, kidneys, and heart. The causes of bacterial pneumonia are diverse and can be categorized into typical and atypical pathogens. Typical bacteria often result in classic pneumonia presentations, while atypical bacteria cause milder symptoms, despite potentially extensive findings on chest imaging. Bacterial pneumonia can also be classified based on patient demographics, such as neonates, children, adults, and the elderly, as well as underlying risk factors like alcohol use, aspiration risk, cystic fibrosis, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, or nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections. Differentiating bacterial pneumonia from other pulmonary diseases is critical, as symptoms can overlap. Diagnostic tools such as chest X-rays, throat cultures, and bacterial sensitivity tests are essential. Conditions that must be ruled out include bronchitis, bronchiolitis obliterans, empyema, lung abscesses, pulmonary carcinomas, bacterial endocarditis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and sinusitis. Epidemiologically, pneumonia is a global health concern, with disproportionately higher mortality rates in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Seasonal variations influence case rates, with Streptococcus pneumoniae infections peaking in winter. Socioeconomic factors, gender, race, and underlying health conditions also play significant roles in disease prevalence. Men are more frequently affected than women, and African Americans have higher rates of bacterial pneumonia compared to Caucasians. Certain medications, such as proton pump inhibitors and ACE inhibitors, may increase susceptibility. Nosocomial pneumonia, often caused by gram-positive cocci like Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and aerobic gram-negative bacilli like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, typically develops within 48 hours of hospital admission. Bacterial pneumonia progresses through stages, including congestion, hepatization, and resolution. Symptoms often include sudden fever, chills, rigors, and cough. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets or contact with contaminated surfaces, followed by self-inoculation through the eyes, nose, or mouth. Complications such as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pleural effusion, sepsis, and shock can arise, influencing prognosis. A thorough patient history is crucial for identifying the underlying cause of pneumonia. Common symptoms include cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain. Specific findings, such as diarrhea, hyponatremia, or anemia, may suggest particular pathogens. Physical examination findings vary depending on disease severity, causative bacteria, and complications. Pulmonary findings and vital sign abnormalities are common, and neurological symptoms like confusion may develop in cases of sepsis. Laboratory findings in bacterial pneumonia typically include elevated white blood cell counts and inflammatory markers like ESR and C-reactive protein. Anemia and thrombocytopenia may also be present. Arterial blood gas analysis often reveals respiratory acidosis. Additional tests, such as gram staining, sputum cultures, blood cultures, and PCR, aid in diagnosis and guide antibiotic selection. Chest X-rays are the gold standard for diagnosing bacterial pneumonia, revealing patterns such as lobar pneumonia, multifocal bronchopneumonia, or interstitial pneumonia. CT scans, while not routinely used, can provide detailed imaging in complex cases or when initial treatments fail. Other imaging modalities, such as ultrasonography, MRI, and lung biopsy, are less commonly employed but may be useful in specific scenarios. Treatment of bacterial pneumonia primarily involves antibiotics, with the choice of agent depending on the causative organism, local resistance patterns, and patient factors. In the UK, amoxicillin is the first-line therapy for community-acquired pneumonia, often combined with clarithromycin. In North America, where atypical pathogens are more common, macrolides like clarithromycin or azithromycin, or fluoroquinolones, are preferred. Hospitalized or immunocompromised patients may require intravenous antibiotics guided by local protocols. Primary prevention strategies include vaccination and management of underlying conditions. Pneumococcal vaccines, such as PCV13 and PPSV23, are recommended for children, older adults, and individuals with chronic health conditions. Annual influenza vaccination is also advised. The cost-effectiveness of antibiotic and corticosteroid therapy has been demonstrated, particularly in community-acquired pneumonia. Emerging therapies aim to address antibiotic resistance and focus on host-directed approaches, including genetic factors and immune responses, to improve outcomes and reduce complications.
